finance.metaTitle: Nvidia Q2 Earnings Beat as AI Chip Demand Surges
finance.metaDescription: Nvidia's fiscal Q2 revenue more than doubled to $96.2 billion, beating estimates, as AI chip demand outstrips supply and hyperscaler spending accelerates.
finance.title: Nvidia's Quarterly Revenue Doubles to $96.2 Billion as AI Chip Demand Outpaces Supply
finance.excerpt: Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter revenue more than doubled to $96.2 billion, beating Wall Street forecasts, as CEO Jensen Huang said the company can only meet about 70% of current AI chip demand.
finance.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of a luminous AI processor connecting data-center racks to rising blocks that suggest surging demand
keyTakeaways: Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter revenue more than doubled year over year to $96.22 billion, with adjusted earnings of $2.22 per share, both topping Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG and FactSet.

Data-center revenue reached $89 billion, up 117% from a year earlier, driven by hyperscaler and enterprise demand for Nvidia's Blackwell architecture, while CEO Jensen Huang said the company can currently supply only about 70% of demand.

Nvidia guided to $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, excluding any China data-center compute revenue, as investors continue to weigh the company's roughly $5 trillion valuation against questions about the durability of AI infrastructure spending.
finance.quote: AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue.

content.text: Nvidia's Results Reinforce the Scale of the AI Buildout

Nvidia closed out its fiscal second quarter with numbers that once again outran Wall Street's models, offering fresh evidence that spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure has yet to slow. The chipmaker reported revenue of $96.22 billion for the three months ended July 26, 2026, more than double the $46.7 billion it posted in the same period a year earlier and well ahead of the roughly $92 billion analysts had penciled in, according to LSEG and FactSet estimates.

GAAP net income came in at $59.69 billion, or $2.46 per diluted share, compared with $26.42 billion, or $1.08 per share, a year earlier. On an adjusted basis, which now includes stock-based compensation, Nvidia earned $2.22 per share, ahead of the roughly $2.09 to $2.10 consensus estimate compiled by analysts. Gross margin held at 75.0%, up from 72.5%-72.7% a year earlier, reflecting a favorable shift toward Nvidia's newer Blackwell Ultra chips.
Data Centers Remain the Engine of Nvidia's Growth

The company's data-center segment, which covers the AI accelerators and systems sold to cloud providers, enterprises and AI labs, generated $89.02 billion in the quarter, up 18% sequentially and 117% from a year earlier. Within that total, hyperscale revenue reached $49 billion, up 13% quarter over quarter, while revenue from Nvidia's other enterprise, AI-native and sovereign customers grew 138% year over year.

"AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue," Huang said in the company's earnings statement, adding on the analyst call that demand across hyperscalers, AI labs and enterprises continues to accelerate.
Demand Still Outstrips What Nvidia Can Supply

Even with record output, Nvidia executives said the company remains unable to fully satisfy customer orders. "Our entire supply chain is challenged," Huang told analysts. "At this point we have supply for 70%. ... Our demand is much higher than that." Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress echoed that view, saying Nvidia's growth outlook for fiscal 2028 would be closer to double the roughly 70% currently projected if supply, rather than demand, were the constraint.

Nvidia's supply commitments, largely tied to memory procurement for its upcoming Vera Rubin platform, more than doubled from $119 billion in the prior quarter to $279 billion, a sign of how far in advance the company is now locking in components to keep pace with orders. Executives noted that tight memory supply is itself a byproduct of the broader AI buildout rather than an unrelated bottleneck.
Guidance Points to Continued Acceleration, With China Excluded

For its fiscal third quarter, Nvidia forecast revenue of about $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, above the roughly $104 billion to $105 billion analysts had expected. If achieved, that would represent year-over-year growth of about 89%, up from the third quarter's 106% growth rate a year earlier, suggesting the company's expansion has not yet plateaued. Nvidia said the guidance assumes no data-center compute revenue from China, a reflection of the current uncertainty around U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips rather than a statement that Nvidia has permanently exited the Chinese market.

Looking further out, Nvidia said it expects revenue for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 to grow by roughly 70%, a target management described as supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained.
Hyperscaler Spending Underpins the Outlook

Kress said capital expenditure among the top five hyperscalers, which include Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta, is expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and climb to about $1.3 trillion in 2027. Nvidia also said its cloud-industry backlog now exceeds $2 trillion. Those figures represent customer spending plans and industry estimates rather than guaranteed Nvidia revenue, though they help explain why the company's own order book has continued to expand.

On the day of the earnings release, Nvidia and Amazon Web Services announced plans to deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia graphics processing units, and said Nvidia chips would also be incorporated into Amazon's fleet of warehouse robots, extending Nvidia's footprint beyond traditional data-center computing.
Nvidia Pushes Further Into Server CPUs

Beyond GPUs, Nvidia is building out a server-processor business, with Kress saying the company expects its CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028, which she said would position Nvidia "as one of the world's leading server CPU suppliers." The company's edge-computing segment, covering chips for personal computers, game consoles and robotics, posted revenue of $7.2 billion, up 27% from a year earlier, a comparatively small but growing part of the business.
Stock Reaction and a Valuation Approaching $5 Trillion

Nvidia shares fell about 1.6% in the regular session ahead of the earnings release, then rebounded in after-hours trading, rising roughly 4% as investors digested the guidance and Huang's growth forecast. The stock remains up more than 12% for the year to date. Nvidia's market capitalization has surged from roughly $400 billion at the end of 2022 to about $5 trillion currently, making it the world's most valuable public company and intensifying scrutiny of whether its growth can continue to justify that valuation.
The Broader Debate Over AI Investment Returns

Nvidia's results land amid a wider argument among investors and economists over whether the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure will eventually generate commensurate economic returns. Bulls point to accelerating enterprise adoption, growing inference workloads and hyperscaler earnings growth as evidence that AI spending is translating into real business value. Skeptics counter that the capital intensity of data-center buildouts, the electricity and infrastructure demands involved, and uncertainty over long-term AI economics could eventually lead to overcapacity or disappointing returns on the trillions being committed.

The AI buildout has also drawn broader public pushback, including objections to data-center expansion in local communities and concerns that rapid AI adoption could displace jobs. Nvidia's own results do not resolve that debate, but they underscore how central the company has become to the AI infrastructure cycle, and how closely its guidance is now watched as a proxy for the health of that broader investment wave.

finance.metaTitle: Bessent, Warsh Split on Who Sets U.S. Borrowing Costs
finance.metaDescription: Treasury's debt buybacks and Fed Chair Warsh's market-driven approach reveal differing views on long-term rates as U.S. debt tops $40 trillion.
finance.title: Bessent's Treasury Buybacks and Warsh's Fed Reveal Two Views on Who Should Price U.S. Debt
finance.excerpt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's move to double debt buybacks and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's preference for market-driven rates reflect competing approaches to long-term Treasury yields as U.S. debt surpasses $40 trillion.
finance.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of diverging paths between a Treasury debt ledger, bond markets and long-term interest rates
keyTakeaways: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has at least doubled the size of Treasury's debt buyback operations, targeting bonds in the 10-to-30-year range after the 30-year yield hit its highest level in roughly 19 years.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has signaled a preference for letting bond markets play a bigger role in setting long-term rates, a stance some analysts see as in tension with Treasury's more interventionist approach.

U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion this month, and economists note that debt-management tools cannot by themselves resolve the upward pressure on yields stemming from persistent federal deficits.
finance.quote: There's very little evidence that Treasuries are oversold right now.

content.text: Two Washington Officials, Two Views on Pricing U.S. Debt

A quiet but consequential disagreement has emerged in Washington over a question with outsized consequences for mortgage rates, corporate borrowing and the federal government's own financing costs: how much should policymakers intervene when bond markets push long-term interest rates higher? Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, both influential voices in setting the price of money in the United States, appear to be answering that question in different ways.

The contrast has sharpened as long-term Treasury yields climbed to multi-decade highs this summer, prompting the Trump administration to take unusual steps to manage bond-market conditions. Whether those measures can meaningfully offset the forces pushing yields upward, including a swelling federal deficit, remains a matter of dispute among economists and bond investors.
Why Long-Term Treasury Yields Became a Flashpoint

The 30-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level in roughly 19 years, predating the 2008 financial crisis, before Treasury's intervention, while the 10-year yield, which heavily influences mortgage rates, approached levels investors and officials alike view as economically and politically uncomfortable. Higher yields on long-term government debt ripple outward: they raise the cost of a 30-year mortgage, push up corporate borrowing costs, and increase the interest the federal government itself must pay to service its debt.

Treasury bond yields move based on a mix of factors, including expectations for inflation and Federal Reserve policy, the pace of economic growth, the sheer volume of new government debt being issued, and what analysts call a term premium, the extra compensation investors demand for the risk of holding long-dated bonds. Analysts have pointed to several forces behind this summer's rise: solid economic growth, persistently elevated inflation, expectations that the Fed could move to raise rates rather than cut them, heavy bond issuance tied in part to AI-related corporate borrowing, and a widening premium tied to concerns about the sustainability of U.S. deficits.
Bessent Turns to Treasury's Debt-Management Toolkit

In mid-August, Treasury announced it would at least double the size of its buyback operations for longer-dated debt, raising the maximum purchase size from $2 billion to at least $4 billion, targeting securities in the 10-year to 30-year range. Treasury said the accelerated buybacks would run from September 9 through November 4. Bessent argued that the rise in yields did not reflect economic fundamentals, and investors interpreted the move as a signal that Washington would not allow the 10-year yield, a key driver of mortgage rates, to approach 5% without a response.

The announcement briefly pushed yields lower: the 30-year yield fell from roughly 5.26% to about 5.18%, and the 10-year yield dropped from around 4.68% to about 4.63%. But the rally proved short-lived. Yields drifted back up in the following sessions as traders weighed the buyback plan against what many view as more structural pressures on the bond market. Bessent has described Treasury's approach as drawing on a broad toolkit, including adjustments to the mix of debt maturities it issues and support for strengthening banks' capacity to intermediate the Treasury market, while maintaining that a predictable, rules-based issuance schedule limits how much Treasury alone can move long-term yields.
Skeptics Say Treasury Is Fighting the Wrong Battle

Not all investors are convinced the buyback strategy addresses the actual source of upward pressure on yields. Will Compernolle, a macro strategist at FHN Financial, said the bond market does not appear structurally impaired. "There's very little evidence that Treasuries are oversold right now," he said, a view echoed by others who argue the rise in yields reflects fundamental economic conditions rather than market dysfunction that Treasury intervention is designed to fix.

Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, who has mentored both Bessent and Warsh earlier in their careers, was more pointed, describing Treasury's approach as "price management" rather than liquidity management, and warning that it could damage Treasury's credibility with investors over time. Traders have also pointed to the U.S. dollar's decline following Bessent's announcement as evidence that attempts to hold down yields can generate pressure elsewhere in financial markets rather than eliminating it.
Warsh Wants Markets to Do More of the Work

Where Bessent has leaned into active intervention, Warsh has signaled a preference for stepping back. He has long been critical of the Federal Reserve's large-scale asset purchases in recent years, arguing that such interventions should be reserved for genuine episodes of market dysfunction rather than used as a routine tool to manage the level of long-term rates. Unlike Treasury, the Fed's toolkit is considerably more powerful: it sets short-term interest rates directly and can buy or sell securities to influence broader financial conditions. Warsh's stated reluctance to use those tools as aggressively as his predecessors marks a deliberate shift in how the Fed relates to bond-market pricing.

That divergence in philosophy is expected to come into focus when Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole address as Fed chair. Investors are looking for reassurance that Warsh will respond decisively to persistent inflation even as he leads a Fed committee that has shown internal division over the appropriate policy path. Stanford finance professor Hanno Lustig has argued in a recent paper that the deeper question dividing officials is whether Treasuries should still be treated as a fundamentally safe asset. Lustig contends that market pricing already reflects growing doubts about that safety, even as policymakers continue to treat yield spikes as evidence of market malfunction rather than legitimate concerns about debt sustainability, a framing that can dull the price signals that would otherwise warn of unsustainable borrowing.
There's very little evidence that Treasuries are oversold right now.
The Fiscal Deficit Limits What Either Approach Can Achieve

Complicating both officials' positions is the scale of the underlying fiscal problem. U.S. gross federal debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time this month, according to Treasury data released alongside the buyback announcement. The Congressional Budget Office has projected a fiscal year 2026 deficit of roughly $1.9 trillion, equivalent to about 5.8% of GDP, well above the 50-year historical average of 3.8%, driven primarily by government spending that continues to outpace long-run norms.

Padhraic Garvey, head of global rates and debt strategy at ING, has described Treasury's unscheduled buybacks as a potential "bazooka" that could be expanded further, and said adjustments to auction sizes for long-dated debt could be Treasury's next move. Molly Brooks, a U.S. rates strategist at TD Securities, said reducing long-end auction sizes is "probably the next move" available to Treasury officials. But most analysts agree that such measures amount to managing the symptoms of the deficit problem rather than solving it. "It'll be very difficult to reduce the deficit without taking some fiscal action," Garvey said, "which requires either higher taxes or lower spending."
What Households, Businesses and Investors Are Watching

For ordinary borrowers, the practical stakes of this debate are straightforward: the 10-year Treasury yield remains the key benchmark for 30-year mortgage rates, while corporate borrowing costs across the economy track movements in longer-dated government debt. Sustained upward pressure on yields, even if temporarily offset by Treasury intervention, could keep financing costs elevated for homebuyers and businesses alike.

In the weeks ahead, investors are likely to watch several signals closely: how markets respond to Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks, whether Treasury follows through on further buyback expansions or auction-size adjustments, incoming inflation and growth data that could shift expectations for Fed policy, and any indication from Congress on fiscal measures that might address the deficit directly. Absent progress on that last front, analysts suggest the underlying tension between market-based price discovery and policy intervention is likely to persist, regardless of which approach prevails in the near term.

finance.metaTitle: Dollar Steadies as Markets Await Warsh's Jackson Hole Talk
finance.metaDescription: The dollar index climbed near an eight-day high after sticky U.S. inflation data, with traders now awaiting Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole address.
finance.title: Dollar Firms Toward Eight-Day High as Sticky Inflation Sets Up Warsh's Jackson Hole Test
finance.excerpt: The U.S. dollar index climbed toward an eight-day high after hotter-than-expected inflation data reinforced bets on a year-end Fed rate move, with investors now turning to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole address for policy signals.
finance.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of a dollar-shaped compass balancing inflation signals against a mountain policy path
keyTakeaways: The dollar index rose to about 99.13, its highest level since August 19, after July inflation data came in hotter than expected and kept alive market bets on a Federal Reserve rate increase by year-end.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole address, scheduled for Friday, is seen as a key test of how the central bank will balance sticky inflation against concerns about Treasury-market intervention and fiscal credibility.

Treasury's expanded debt-buyback program and record U.S. government debt have revived concerns about fiscal credibility, a factor analysts say could limit how far the dollar can rally even if the Fed signals a firmer policy stance.
finance.quote: Chairman Kevin Warsh's upcoming speech at Jackson Hole will be the ultimate test.

content.text: Dollar Climbs Toward an Eight-Day High

The U.S. dollar strengthened this week, with the dollar index rising about 0.2% to roughly 99.13, its highest level since August 19, as hotter-than-expected inflation data reinforced the case that the Federal Reserve may need to keep policy restrictive for longer. Against the yen, the dollar traded near 159.23, having given back much of the gains it registered after last month's joint U.S.-Japan currency intervention but remaining well above the multi-decade low of roughly 164 per dollar reached earlier in the crisis.

The move builds on a partial recovery from a rough stretch for the greenback: the dollar index touched its lowest level since May earlier this week, pressured largely by the Treasury Department's decision to sharply expand its buybacks of longer-dated government debt, a move that pulled bond yields lower and, with them, some of the dollar's recent support.
Sticky Inflation Reshapes the Rate Outlook

The Commerce Department's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.7% in the 12 months through July, matching June's pace and coming in above the 3.6% economists had forecast. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, held at 3.3% annually. Both readings remain well above the Fed's 2% target, reinforcing market expectations that the central bank will need more evidence of cooling prices before easing policy.

Westpac economist Ryan Wells said the inflation data kept alive market expectations for a Fed rate move by year-end, though he noted that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's upcoming address would be decisive. "Chairman Kevin Warsh's upcoming speech at Jackson Hole will be the ultimate test," Wells said in a note. Traders have priced in little chance of a move at the Fed's September meeting but see a substantially higher probability, in the range of roughly 70% by some estimates, of a quarter-point rate increase by December, according to market pricing tracked through futures markets.
Why Jackson Hole Has Become the Key Catalyst

Warsh is scheduled to deliver his first keynote address as Fed chair at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday, an event this year themed around financial innovation and payments policy. Since taking office earlier this year, Warsh has largely declined to offer explicit forward guidance, a departure from his predecessors that some analysts argue has itself contributed to elevated volatility in bond markets. His remarks will be closely parsed both for clues on the Fed's approach to inflation and for any indication of how the central bank views the Treasury's recent market interventions.

Analysts caution that Warsh is not expected to provide explicit guidance on the September policy decision, consistent with his approach since taking the role. Even so, currency strategists say any deviation from his typically cautious tone could trigger a meaningful reaction: the dollar index has historically moved by roughly half a percentage point to more than a percentage point in the hours following past Jackson Hole addresses.
U.S. Growth Offers the Dollar Additional Support

Beyond the inflation debate, the dollar continues to draw support from the relative strength of the U.S. economy. Second-quarter GDP growth was confirmed at an annualized 1.5%, while separate data showed consumer spending revised higher and business investment, particularly around artificial intelligence infrastructure, remaining robust. Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman, said the U.S. economy's continued outperformance relative to other major economies remains the dollar's biggest source of support, adding that he expects the Fed to leave rates unchanged for the remainder of the year, a view that runs somewhat counter to current market pricing for a possible December move.
Fiscal Concerns Remain an Overhang on the Dollar

Even as the dollar firms on rate expectations, its gains face a structural headwind from renewed questions about U.S. fiscal credibility. The Treasury Department's decision to at least double its buybacks of longer-dated government debt, aimed at containing a rise in long-term borrowing costs, has stoked concerns among some investors that Washington is prioritizing near-term market stability over addressing the underlying growth in government debt, which surpassed $40 trillion this month. Some analysts have said the episode has revived discussion about long-term dollar debasement risk, though this reflects a debate among market participants rather than a settled conclusion about the currency's fundamental value.

One currency strategist, discussing the outlook on condition of anonymity, said the combination of shifting Fed rate expectations and fiscal uncertainty creates a difficult balance for the dollar: "I don't expect the dollar to make new highs, because the risk of a more dovish Fed repricing and the lack of U.S. fiscal credibility are two big headwinds." The 10-year Treasury yield has hovered near 4.7% in recent sessions, with investors still working through how much of the move reflects inflation and growth expectations versus concern about the sustainability of federal borrowing.
Yen, Euro and Other Currencies Face Their Own Drivers

The Japanese yen has been shaped by its own set of considerations. Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino said this week that timely rate increases could help the central bank avoid a more disruptive inflation spike later, though he stopped short of signaling an imminent move. Sho Suzuki, a market analyst at Matsui Securities, said Himino's comments on upside price risks were not read as especially dovish, though the absence of clearer signaling leaves open the possibility that the yen could face renewed downward pressure. The yen has retraced part of the gains it registered following last month's joint currency intervention by U.S. and Japanese authorities.

The euro has held broadly steady near $1.165, supported in part by improving eurozone business activity, with composite purchasing managers' data climbing to its highest level since November. The British pound has traded with modest softness against the dollar. The Canadian dollar, meanwhile, has held relatively steady even as trade tensions between Ottawa and Washington escalated following the breakdown of talks and the introduction of new tariffs on both sides, with President Donald Trump saying this week it was "time to teach Canada" a lesson, a comment that underscores the political friction but has not yet produced a clear directional move in the currency pair.
What Could Determine the Dollar's Next Move

With Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks, weekly jobless claims data, and the ongoing fallout from Treasury's debt-buyback program all in play this week, currency strategists say the dollar's near-term path will likely hinge on whether incoming signals reinforce or challenge current market pricing for Fed policy. A hawkish surprise from Warsh could extend the dollar's recovery, while renewed doubts about fiscal credibility or a more dovish tone could quickly reverse recent gains. For now, most analysts describe the dollar's rebound as a stabilization within a broader range rather than the start of a sustained rally.

finance.metaTitle: Wall Street Eyes Nvidia After Hot Inflation Print
finance.metaDescription: Wall Street closed slightly lower after sticky inflation data, but Nvidia's blowout earnings and guidance revived the AI trade ahead of Jackson Hole.
finance.title: Wall Street Steadies After Sticky Inflation as Nvidia's Earnings Reset the AI Narrative
finance.excerpt: Major U.S. indexes closed marginally lower after hotter-than-expected inflation data, but Nvidia's stronger-than-expected earnings and guidance, released after the bell, quickly reshaped the outlook for technology stocks heading into the Fed's Jackson Hole symposium.
finance.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of market charts balancing an inflation gauge with an illuminated AI chip
keyTakeaways: The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all closed marginally lower on Wednesday after July PCE inflation held at 3.7% annually, above the 3.6% economists expected, keeping the Federal Reserve's policy path uncertain ahead of its September meeting.

Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter revenue more than doubled to $96.22 billion and its guidance of $108 billion for the current quarter beat estimates, sending shares up roughly 4% to 7% in after-hours and premarket trading and lifting semiconductor stocks broadly.

Traders were pricing in roughly a 38% to 44% probability of a Fed rate increase at the September meeting following the inflation data, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole address on Friday seen as the next major catalyst for rate expectations.
finance.quote: It wasn't enough to shift the balance for September's meeting, but if subsequent data point in the same direction, the Fed may feel more pressure to move off the sidelines.

content.text: Major Indexes Close Marginally Lower on Sticky Inflation

Wall Street's major indexes ended Wednesday's session with modest losses after a government inflation report came in slightly hotter than economists had forecast, leaving investors cautious just hours before Nvidia's closely watched earnings release. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 113.52 points, or 0.21%, to close at 53,463.88. The S&P 500 slipped 1.58 points, or 0.02%, to 7,675.70, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 21.10 points, or 0.08%, to 26,130.20.

The modest declines reflected a market in a holding pattern rather than one reacting sharply to bad news. Much of the day's trading activity was concentrated around positioning ahead of two events investors viewed as far more consequential: Nvidia's after-the-bell earnings report and Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's upcoming address at the Jackson Hole symposium.
Why the Inflation Data Kept the Fed's Path Uncertain

The Commerce Department's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, showed prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through July, matching June's pace but coming in above the 3.6% economists had expected. Core PCE, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, held steady at 3.3% annually. Both readings remain well above the Fed's 2% inflation target, a threshold the index has now exceeded for well over five years.

Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, said the report alone was unlikely to change the calculus for the Fed's next meeting but could add pressure over time. "It wasn't enough to shift the balance for September's meeting, but if subsequent data point in the same direction, the Fed may feel more pressure to move off the sidelines," she said. Traders' expectations for a rate increase at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting hovered in a range of roughly 38% to 44% following the data, according to different readings of market pricing tracked through CME's FedWatch tool, up modestly from levels seen before the report.
Markets Brace for Warsh's First Jackson Hole Address

Attention has increasingly shifted to Warsh's keynote speech at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, scheduled for Friday. It will be his first major address since becoming Fed chair, and investors are watching for signals on how he plans to balance persistent inflation against a Treasury market that has recently shown signs of strain. Warsh has generally avoided offering explicit forward guidance since taking the role, a departure from his predecessors that some strategists say has itself contributed to volatility in bond markets.

Greg Tuorto, head of U.S. small and midcap investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said the uncertainty was less about any acute economic problem than about the range of possible policy paths. "There is no crisis, it is more about expectations or guidance we are going to get from the Fed and what the Treasury is trying to do. That blends to some uncertainty and basically increases the risk premium," he said, adding that corporate fundamentals remained a bright spot: "On the positive side, the underlying economic environment is really good. Earnings for the companies that we own and some of the larger cap companies are standout."
Nvidia's Results Reset the AI Narrative

Nvidia shares had drifted 1.6% lower during Wednesday's regular session as investors waited nervously for the chipmaker's results, with some fearing that anything short of a blowout report could reignite doubts about the durability of AI infrastructure spending. Those concerns eased quickly once the numbers were released after the close: Nvidia reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion, more than double the $46.7 billion reported a year earlier and well above the roughly $92 billion analysts had expected.

Adjusted earnings came in at $2.22 per share, ahead of the roughly $2.09 to $2.10 consensus estimate, while data-center revenue, the segment covering AI accelerators sold to cloud providers and enterprises, rose 117% year over year to $89 billion. CEO Jensen Huang said demand continues to outstrip what the company can supply, telling analysts that Nvidia currently has capacity to meet only about 70% of demand. For the current quarter, Nvidia guided to revenue of roughly $108 billion, ahead of Wall Street's roughly $104 billion to $105 billion estimate, a forecast that implies growth of about 89% from a year earlier.

Nvidia shares rose roughly 4% in after-hours trading following the report and extended those gains into premarket trading Thursday, climbing further as investors digested the guidance. The reaction rippled across the sector: other chipmakers including Marvell Technology and Micron Technology also advanced in premarket trading, while South Korea's KOSPI index, home to major memory-chip suppliers, closed notably higher, reflecting how closely Nvidia's results are tied to sentiment across the broader semiconductor supply chain.
Other Corporate Movers Shaped Wednesday's Session

Beyond the AI trade, several individual stocks moved on company-specific news. Healthcare shares were the weakest sector in the S&P 500, falling about 1%, with Moderna dropping 5.8% after a sharp gain a day earlier, though the stock remained well above levels seen before the company disclosed promising late-stage cancer vaccine trial data alongside partner Merck. Meta Platforms rose almost 1.1%, leading gains among megacap technology names after agreeing to pay up to $18 billion and make significant changes to Facebook and Instagram to resolve claims brought by U.S. states over harm to children. Apple added 1.1%.

Elsewhere, Intuit fell 3.2% after the tax-software maker issued annual revenue guidance below Wall Street's expectations, while J.M. Smucker gained 4.3% after forecasting a smaller-than-expected decline in annual sales. CrowdStrike shares, which had risen about 2% ahead of its own results, climbed further after the cybersecurity firm posted a record quarter and raised its annual revenue forecast, reinforcing investor confidence that AI-adjacent software companies can grow alongside chip-focused peers rather than being displaced by them.
Treasury Yields and Broader Risk Factors Remain in Play

Treasury yields, which had climbed to multi-year highs the previous week on concerns tied to rising government debt, inflation, and geopolitical risk, have since retreated somewhat after the Treasury Department announced an expanded debt buyback program aimed at supporting the long end of the bond market. Elevated long-term yields matter directly for equity valuations, particularly for high-growth technology companies: when yields rise, the future earnings that justify richer stock valuations are discounted more heavily, making growth stocks more sensitive to shifts in the rate outlook than the broader market.

Separately, a report citing an Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesperson indicated that Iran and Oman had reached an understanding on sharing the Strait of Hormuz and its associated revenue, a development that has contributed to easing oil prices this week after a sustained period of elevated energy costs tied to the broader Middle East conflict. Lower oil prices, if sustained, could ease some of the inflationary pressure that has kept the Fed cautious about cutting rates.
Market Breadth Reflected a Cautious Undertone

Beneath the narrow moves in the major indexes, market breadth on Wednesday leaned negative. Declining stocks outnumbered advancers by a ratio of roughly 1.16-to-1 on the New York Stock Exchange, with 144 stocks hitting new 52-week highs against 66 new lows. On the Nasdaq, decliners outpaced advancers by about 1.38-to-1, and the exchange recorded 68 new highs against 75 new lows. Trading volume across U.S. exchanges totaled 14.2 billion shares, below the 20-day moving average of 16.2 billion, consistent with a market that was largely waiting for the two catalysts, Nvidia's results and Friday's Jackson Hole address, to provide clearer direction.
What Investors Are Watching Next

With Nvidia's results now in hand, the market's attention shifts fully to Warsh's Friday remarks and to whether he offers any signal, explicit or implied, about the Fed's tolerance for inflation running persistently above target. Weekly jobless claims data due before Thursday's opening bell will offer another data point on labor-market health. Investors are likely to weigh Nvidia's evidence of continued AI infrastructure demand against the unresolved question of how the Fed will balance sticky inflation, elevated Treasury yields, and a fiscal backdrop that continues to draw scrutiny from bond investors.

business.metaTitle: Sticky Inflation, Slower Growth and the Fed’s Next Move
business.metaDescription: July inflation and the latest second-quarter GDP estimate point in different directions. Here is what the public data establish and what remains uncertain.
business.title: Sticky Inflation and Slower Growth Complicate the Fed’s Next Move
business.excerpt: Annual U.S. inflation stayed at 3.7% in July while the second estimate put real second-quarter GDP growth at 1.5%, down from 2.1% in the first quarter—an awkward combination for the Federal Reserve.
business.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of a persistent price gauge beside a narrowing but brighter economic growth path
keyTakeaways: Annual PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, held at 3.7% in July, above forecasts of 3.6% and still well above the central bank's 2% target, while core PCE was unchanged at 3.3%.

Second-quarter consumer spending was revised up to a 3.4% annualized pace, business investment stayed strong on continued AI-related spending, and corporate profits posted their second-largest quarterly jump on record.

Markets have modestly raised the odds of a September rate move following the data, but a majority of Fed officials left rates unchanged at their last meeting, and no decision has been made ahead of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech.
business.quote: This wasn't just any PCE report — it was the PCE report before Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote, which could make or break the resurrection of the debasement trade.

content.text: Inflation Holds Steady Just Before Warsh's Jackson Hole Debut

Fresh government data this week showed U.S. inflation refusing to budge even as other indicators pointed to an economy gathering momentum, a combination that is complicating the Federal Reserve's calculations heading into a pivotal speech by its chairman. The timing was pointed: the inflation report landed just two days before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh was due to deliver his first keynote address at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday, an appearance investors and bond traders have been anticipating for weeks.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the inflation gauge the Fed uses to guide policy, rose 3.7% in the 12 months through July, matching June's annual rate and coming in above the 3.6% economists had forecast. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.2% in July after slipping 0.1% in June, also above the 0.1% increase economists expected.
Core Inflation Still Running Well Above Target

Core PCE, which strips out volatile food and energy costs and is closely watched by policymakers as a gauge of underlying price pressure, held at 3.3% annually, in line with expectations, while rising 0.2% for the month after a 0.1% gain in June. Both measures remain far above the Fed's longstanding 2% inflation target, a threshold annual PCE has now exceeded for more than five consecutive years.

Forecasting firm Inflation Insights founder Omair Sharif said the underlying monthly core reading, before rounding, came in at roughly 0.246%, just shy of rounding up to 0.3% and equivalent to an annualized pace of nearly 3%. "This is data that supports a hike," he said.
Consumer Spending Cools Even as Incomes Outpace Prices

The same report showed consumer spending decelerating modestly in July and essentially flat once adjusted for inflation, even as personal income grew faster than prices. Some economists read the income gain as a potential cushion for spending later in the year, though at least one analyst noted early signs of "consumer fatigue" in the flat real spending figure.
Growth Signals Firm Up: Durable Goods, AI Spending and GDP Revisions

Separate data released alongside the inflation report painted a more upbeat picture of economic momentum. Orders for major capital goods rebounded in July, led by transportation equipment, while shipments of core durable goods pointed to continued brisk business investment tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Bureau of Economic Analysis also left its estimate of annualized second-quarter GDP growth unchanged at 1.5% but revised second-quarter consumer spending growth up to 3.4% from an initially reported 3.2%, underscoring the resilience of household demand, which accounts for roughly two-thirds of U.S. economic output.

Growth in final sales to private domestic purchasers, a measure combining consumer and business investment spending that is often used as a cleaner read on underlying demand, was revised up to 4.2%, the strongest pace since early 2023, from a previously reported 3.9%. Nationwide chief economist Kathy Bostjancic said the July spending and durable-goods data point to real GDP growth of at least 3% in the third quarter, double the second quarter's pace.
Corporate Profits Post Near-Record Jump

Corporate profits climbed by $400.9 billion in the second quarter, following a $74.4 billion increase in the first quarter, marking the second-largest quarterly jump on record behind only the third quarter of 2020. Economists have linked much of the surge to a corporate tax overhaul that took effect earlier this year. On the income side of the ledger, gross domestic income rose 2.2%, up from 1.2% in the first quarter, while gross domestic output, an average of GDP and GDI that some economists consider a more complete gauge of activity, grew at a 1.8% rate, up from 1.7% previously.
Tariffs and the Lingering Iran Conflict Complicate the Inflation Picture

Inflation's path this year has been shaped heavily by factors outside the Fed's direct control. Annual PCE inflation spiked to a three-year high of 4.1% in May after the United States and Israel launched air strikes against Iran in late February, an escalation that disrupted roughly a fifth of global oil supplies and pushed energy prices sharply higher. Six months on, the conflict has not been resolved, though the intensity of fighting has eased and both oil prices and broader inflation have retreated from their spring peaks.

Tariff policy is adding a further layer of uncertainty. Trade talks between the United States and Canada, its second-largest trading partner, broke down recently, resulting in new tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian imports. Economists have also pointed to the broader wave of import tariffs introduced since last year as a factor that interrupted inflation's earlier decline from a 7.2% peak in mid-2022.
What It Means for the Fed's Next Move

The Fed has held its benchmark federal funds rate at 3.50%-3.75% since its last cut in December 2025, resisting pressure from President Donald Trump to lower borrowing costs. Minutes from the Fed's July meeting showed several policymakers arguing that rate hikes would likely be necessary if inflation failed to decline, even as the majority voted to hold rates steady. Following the July PCE data, market-implied odds of a rate increase at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting, as tracked by tools such as CME FedWatch, rose modestly, though estimates from different sources varied, ranging from roughly 40% to 44%, up from about 36% before the report. Such figures reflect financial-market expectations rather than any Fed decision, and can shift quickly with new data.

Fitch Ratings' head of U.S. economics, Olu Sonola, said the inflation data underscored the scale of the Fed's task. "As Jackson Hole beckons, the Fed's challenge is clear: it still has considerable ground to cover before markets see 2% inflation as a credible outcome rather than a distant aspiration," he said.

All Eyes on Warsh's Jackson Hole Address

Since taking over as Fed chair in May, Warsh has largely avoided offering explicit forward guidance, preferring to let incoming data and market pricing set expectations, an approach some analysts argue has itself contributed to recent volatility in long-term Treasury yields, which have climbed to levels last seen before the 2007-2008 financial crisis. His Friday address at Jackson Hole is expected to be closely parsed for any signal on how the central bank plans to balance stubborn inflation against signs of a reaccelerating economy, though officials caution that no policy decision will be made before the September meeting.

business.metaTitle: Oil Slides on Iran-Qatar Talks, Hormuz Hopes
business.metaDescription: Brent and WTI extended a multi-day slide as Qatar relaunched Iran talks and an Iran-Oman deal raised hopes for eased Strait of Hormuz supply disruptions.
business.title: Oil Prices Extend Slide as Qatar Relaunches Iran Talks and Hormuz Tensions Ease Slightly
business.excerpt: Brent and WTI crude fell for a fourth and fifth straight session respectively as Qatar's prime minister headed to Tehran and a new Iran-Oman understanding on the Strait of Hormuz fueled hopes of easing Middle East supply disruptions.
business.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of oil tankers passing a narrow strait as diplomatic talks ease a supply-risk gauge
keyTakeaways: Brent crude fell toward $86-87 a barrel and WTI toward $80-81 a barrel this week, extending a multi-session losing streak as diplomatic activity around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz intensified.

Iran and Oman have reportedly reached an understanding on sharing the strait's waters and revenues and are discussing a maritime corridor, but Tehran has cautioned that fully reopening the waterway requires more than an agreement with Oman alone.

Qatar's prime minister traveled to Iran to relaunch talks aimed at ending the nearly six-month conflict, while analysts say markets are pricing in improved shipping prospects rather than a full return to pre-conflict oil flows.
business.quote: At the heart of the dispute remains Iran's nuclear programme and that is unlikely to be resolved quickly ... the risk of prolonged uncertainty remains.

content.text: Crude Prices Fall for a Fourth Straight Session

Crude oil extended a multi-day decline this week as traders weighed a fresh round of diplomacy aimed at easing tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that has become the central flashpoint of the Middle East conflict now approaching its sixth month. Brent crude slipped toward the $86-to-$87-a-barrel range, marking a fourth consecutive session of losses, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate fell toward the $80-to-$81 range in its fifth straight down day, according to data tracked by Trading Economics and other market sources.

The declines mark a shift in sentiment after weeks in which prices had been supported by fears that renewed fighting could choke off Gulf oil exports entirely. Traders are now positioning for the possibility, though not the certainty, that shipping through Hormuz could gradually normalize.
Why the Strait of Hormuz Is Central to the Story

The Strait of Hormuz sits between Iran and Oman and serves as the primary maritime corridor for oil and liquefied natural gas exports from major Gulf producers, including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Qatar. Before the conflict began in late February, the strait handled roughly one-fifth of global daily oil and LNG supply, making any disruption there one of the most consequential risks to global energy markets. Its narrow width has long made it a strategic chokepoint, and control over passage through it has become a central point of leverage for Iran during the conflict.
Qatar Relaunches Diplomacy as Iran and Oman Reach a Partial Understanding

Qatar's prime minister traveled to Iran this week to relaunch talks aimed at ending the conflict, which has now run for nearly six months with active fighting largely paused but no comprehensive diplomatic breakthrough achieved. Qatar has said it is continuing its mediation role between the warring parties.

Separately, a senior Iranian source said Iran and Oman were working to finalize an agreement covering how the two countries would share the strait's waters and related revenues, after Iran's Revolutionary Guards indicated the two sides had agreed on a framework for dividing the waterway. Technical discussions between Tehran and Muscat have reportedly continued around establishing what has been described as a temporary joint maritime corridor, with talks extending toward a more permanent arrangement covering administration of the strait, information-sharing, traffic management and maritime security services.
Tehran Signals Limits to Any Deal

Despite the reported progress with Oman, Iranian officials have cautioned that a bilateral understanding with Muscat alone would not be sufficient to fully reopen the strait to normal traffic, given the broader dispute with the United States and unresolved questions over Iran's nuclear program. It also remains unclear whether Washington would accept any arrangement over Hormuz that excludes direct U.S. involvement.

President Donald Trump said this week that roughly 10 million barrels of oil had passed through Hormuz on a single day, while reiterating earlier claims that mines placed in the waterway during the conflict had been cleared. The U.S. has halted its strikes on Iran for roughly a month, shifting toward economic pressure rather than military action, a change that has itself fed investor expectations of an eventual easing in Gulf supply disruptions.
What Shipping Data Actually Shows

Shipping traffic through the strait ticked up slightly this week even as the diplomatic standoff continued, according to tracking data cited by market reports, though the increase has been incremental rather than a wholesale return to pre-conflict volumes. The U.S. Energy Information Administration has separately said it does not expect Middle East oil production to return to near pre-conflict levels until early 2027 and has projected Brent to average around $87 a barrel for 2026, underscoring that the market's baseline expectation remains one of gradual, not immediate, recovery.
Analysts Say Markets Are Pricing Hope, Not Certainty

Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, said the recent price weakness reflects growing expectations that a deal could increase shipping volumes through Hormuz, though he cautioned that a full recovery in flows would take time even under an optimistic scenario. "If Hormuz were to reopen more fully, a further leg lower in crude is possible, but the market is unlikely to price a complete return to pre-conflict levels overnight," Waterer said.

Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova, pointed to the unresolved dispute over Iran's nuclear program as the underlying obstacle to a lasting resolution. "At the heart of the dispute remains Iran's nuclear programme and that is unlikely to be resolved quickly ... Iran also understands the importance of its geographical position and the leverage that the Strait of Hormuz provides, so the risk of prolonged uncertainty remains," she said.
If Hormuz were to reopen more fully, a further leg lower in crude is possible, but the market is unlikely to price a complete return to pre-conflict levels overnight.
Inventories and Broader Supply Signals

U.S. inventory data released this week showed crude stockpiles were little changed, while gasoline and distillate inventories fell to seasonal lows, a signal that domestic demand has remained resilient even as the broader market focuses on Middle East supply risk. OPEC crude output, meanwhile, remains constrained by the conflict, with some analysts noting that a meaningful increase in group production is unlikely until traffic through Hormuz normalizes in both directions.
What Comes Next for Energy Markets

Traders are likely to remain focused on the outcome of Qatar's renewed mediation effort, the pace of technical talks between Iran and Oman over the strait's administration, and any signal from Washington on whether it would accept an arrangement that does not directly involve the United States. Given the string of false starts and reversals over the course of the conflict, analysts caution that oil prices could swing sharply in either direction depending on how the coming days of diplomacy unfold, with a durable resolution to the underlying dispute over Iran's nuclear program still seen as the key unresolved variable.

business.metaTitle: What Nvidia’s Forecast Says About the AI Trade
business.metaDescription: Nvidia’s earnings and forecast renewed enthusiasm for AI-linked stocks. The more useful question is how broad and durable that market response becomes.
business.title: What Nvidia’s Forecast Says About the AI Trade
business.excerpt: Nasdaq 100 futures jumped after Nvidia's strong earnings and guidance, along with beats from Salesforce and CrowdStrike, renewed investor enthusiasm for AI-related stocks even as Fed rate uncertainty and Treasury-yield concerns lingered.
business.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of an AI processor powering a market path while investors weigh growth against concentration risk
keyTakeaways: Nasdaq 100 futures rose about 1% and Nvidia gained roughly 6-7% in premarket trading after the chipmaker forecast continued strong AI demand alongside earnings from Salesforce and CrowdStrike that also beat Wall Street estimates.

Salesforce jumped more than 11% in premarket trading after raising its outlook and reporting a multibillion-dollar gain tied to its stake in AI startup Anthropic, while CrowdStrike rose after posting a record quarter and lifting its own guidance.

Investors remain focused on Federal Reserve policy, with markets pricing roughly a 40% chance of a September rate move following hotter-than-expected inflation data, ahead of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole address.
business.quote: Nvidia's results validate the AI infrastructure trade, but they are not a signal to indiscriminately chase everything labeled AI.

content.text: Technology Futures Lead the Market Higher

U.S. stock-index futures tied to technology shares outperformed the broader market this week after a trio of closely watched earnings reports from Nvidia, Salesforce and CrowdStrike reinforced the case that demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure and software remains robust. Nasdaq 100 futures rose roughly 1%, while S&P 500 futures gained a more modest 0.4% to 0.5% and Dow futures were little changed, underscoring how concentrated the rally has been in technology-heavy names rather than the market as a whole.

The moves followed a subdued session on Wall Street a day earlier, when major indexes closed largely flat as investors awaited Nvidia's results and digested a slightly hotter-than-expected reading on inflation.
Nvidia's Guidance Reframes the AI Spending Debate

Nvidia shares rose roughly 6% to 7% in premarket trading after the company reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion, more than double a year earlier, and issued third-quarter guidance of about $108 billion, ahead of analyst expectations. Chief Executive Jensen Huang told investors demand continues to run well above what the company can currently supply, citing constraints tied to memory-component availability even as Nvidia works to expand its supplier relationships.

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets, said the significance of the report went beyond the headline numbers. "The biggest positive was management effectively telling investors that AI demand remains supply-constrained even at this scale... That is a powerful counter to the narrative that the AI capex cycle is already peaking," Chanana said. She added a note of caution, however: "Nvidia's results validate the AI infrastructure trade, but they are not a signal to indiscriminately chase everything labeled AI."
Semiconductor Stocks Ride Nvidia's Momentum

Nvidia's results lifted chipmakers broadly in premarket trading. Marvell Technology rose roughly 5% to 6%, Micron Technology gained more than 4%, and Broadcom added to recent gains, as investors bet that strong AI accelerator demand would flow through to companies supplying networking chips, memory and other components used in AI data centers. Storage-focused firms Sandisk and Western Digital also advanced, reflecting renewed attention to the memory-supply constraints Nvidia itself flagged as a bottleneck to faster growth.

The rally extended overseas as well, with South Korea's KOSPI index, home to major memory-chip producers, closing about 1.5% higher, a sign that Nvidia's results were read as a positive signal for the broader global semiconductor supply chain rather than a company-specific event.
Software Earnings Ease Fears of AI Disruption

Software companies added a second leg to the rally. Salesforce shares jumped more than 11% in premarket trading after the company raised its annual revenue and profit outlook and reported second-quarter revenue of $11.35 billion, slightly ahead of the roughly $11.32 billion analysts had expected, according to LSEG data. The results were boosted in part by a roughly $2.6 billion gain tied to Salesforce's investment stake in AI company Anthropic. Salesforce also introduced a new integration combining its platform with Anthropic's Claude AI models.

CrowdStrike rose roughly 8% to 9% after the cybersecurity firm reported a record quarter and raised its annual revenue forecast, topping second-quarter earnings estimates. Together, the two reports helped calm investor concerns that generative AI tools could erode demand for traditional enterprise software, a worry that had weighed on software valuations relative to semiconductor stocks seen as more direct AI beneficiaries. Other software names, including ServiceNow and Oracle, gained roughly 2% each in sympathy.
AI Winners Are Not Uniform Across the Market

Analysts have cautioned that the AI trade is not a monolith. Companies supplying the physical infrastructure for AI, chips, memory, networking equipment and data-center hardware, have generally captured the earliest and most direct financial benefits of the AI buildout. Software companies, by contrast, face a more mixed picture: some, like Salesforce and CrowdStrike, are demonstrating that they can integrate AI features into existing products without undermining revenue, while questions persist more broadly about whether generative AI tools could eventually pressure pricing or reduce demand for certain categories of software.
The Federal Reserve Remains a Parallel Storyline

Even as AI-related earnings dominated trading, monetary policy continued to shape the broader market backdrop. A reading of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, came in slightly above expectations for July, holding at an annual pace of 3.7%. That report modestly raised market-implied odds of a Federal Reserve rate increase at the central bank's September meeting, with probabilities tracked by CME's FedWatch tool running in the range of roughly 40% in the wake of the data, up from about 36% beforehand. A separate weekly reading on jobless claims was scheduled for release before Thursday's opening bell, offering another data point for traders assessing the health of the labor market.
Treasury Yields and Jackson Hole in Focus

Concerns about rising U.S. government debt and inflation pressures tied in part to the ongoing conflict involving Iran had pushed Treasury yields to multi-year highs in recent weeks, prompting the Treasury Department to announce supportive measures aimed at calming the bond market. That backdrop has sharpened investor attention on Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who is scheduled to deliver his first policy address as chair at the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole symposium. Since taking over the role earlier this year, Warsh has largely avoided explicit forward guidance, leaving market participants to parse incoming data, including this week's earnings and inflation reports, for clues about the likely path of interest rates.

Taken together, the week's developments illustrate a market trying to hold two ideas at once: confidence that AI infrastructure spending has further room to run, based on demand signals from companies like Nvidia, Salesforce and CrowdStrike, alongside continued uncertainty over how persistent inflation and elevated Treasury yields might ultimately shape Federal Reserve policy and, by extension, valuations across the technology sector.

business.metaTitle: Canada Drops Seafood From New U.S. Tariff Package
business.metaDescription: Canada removed seafood and fish products from its $20 billion retaliatory tariff list on U.S. goods, citing industry feedback ahead of the Sept. 8 start date.
business.title: Canada Carves Seafood Out of Its Retaliatory Tariffs as U.S. Trade Dispute Escalates
business.excerpt: Canada removed seafood and fish products from planned counter-tariffs after announcing measures covering C$27.6 billion in U.S. goods in response to new 50% American tariffs.
business.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of seafood shipments moving through changing tariff barriers and cross-border trade routes
keyTakeaways: Canada's Department of Finance removed seafood and fish products from its list of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods, citing industry feedback aimed at limiting economic harm.

The exclusion came a day after Canada unveiled counter-tariffs worth about $20 billion (roughly C$27.6 billion) on more than 700 U.S. products, set to take effect September 8 at rates of 15%, 25% and 50%.

The retaliatory measures match new U.S. tariffs of 50% on a range of Canadian goods that took effect after trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down, with dairy, steel, aluminum, appliances and other goods still covered.
business.quote: Based on feedback, we have made select adjustments to protect against economic harms, including removing seafood and fish products from our list of counter tariffs.

content.text: Ottawa Adjusts Its Retaliation Package Within a Day

Canada's Department of Finance pulled seafood and fish products from its newly announced list of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. imports, just one day after unveiling counter-measures covering roughly $20 billion worth of American goods. The department said in a statement posted on social media that the change followed direct input from Canadian businesses. "Based on feedback, we have made select adjustments to protect against economic harms, including removing seafood and fish products from our list of counter tariffs," the department said.

The exemption is a narrow but telling adjustment to a much larger retaliatory package that Ottawa says is designed to match Washington's latest tariffs dollar for dollar. It illustrates how quickly Canadian officials have been willing to revise even freshly announced trade measures once industry concerns are raised.
How the Latest Round of Tariffs Began

The exemption comes amid a rapidly escalating trade dispute between the two countries. The United States imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian imports over the weekend after trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed. In response, Canada's Finance Minister, François-Philippe Champagne, announced on Tuesday that Canada would match the U.S. measures "dollar for dollar, rate for rate," unveiling counter-tariffs covering more than 700 American products worth close to $20 billion, or about C$27.6 billion, in annual trade.

Those retaliatory tariffs are structured in three tiers, 15%, 25% and 50%, mirroring the rates the U.S. has applied to comparable Canadian goods. Canada's countermeasures are set to take effect on September 8 and are concentrated on sectors that officials said have been directly targeted by U.S. tariffs, including steel, aluminum, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Why Seafood Was Singled Out for Removal

While the Finance Department's statement did not detail the specific industry input behind the seafood exemption, Canada's fish and seafood sector has a level of trade exposure to the United States that makes it especially sensitive to cross-border tariff actions. Industry representatives, including the Fisheries Council of Canada, have previously noted that a majority of Canadian seafood exports, historically estimated at around two-thirds, are shipped to the U.S. market, leaving processors and harvesters with limited ability to quickly redirect sales elsewhere if tariffs raise costs or reduce competitiveness.

That heavy reliance on a single export market means retaliatory tariffs affecting seafood could carry outsized consequences for coastal economies, including fishing and processing communities in provinces such as Newfoundland and Labrador and Nova Scotia, where the seafood sector is a significant employer. By removing seafood from its list, Ottawa appears to be attempting to limit the domestic economic fallout of its own retaliatory measures rather than simply mirroring every category the U.S. has targeted.
What Remains on Canada's Tariff List

Despite the seafood carve-out, Canada's broader retaliation package remains substantial. Officials have said the countermeasures still cover dairy products, steel and aluminum, home appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper goods, electronics, tools, furniture and clothing. Steel and aluminum face the steepest rate, with Canada doubling its duties to 50% to match the equivalent U.S. tariff on those metals. According to Canadian officials, the retaliatory tariffs, calculated using 2024 trade data, apply to goods representing close to 4.5% of Canada's total imports from the United States.
The Broader Toll on Cross-Border Trade

The dispute marks a further deterioration in a trade relationship long built on largely tariff-free access under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The U.S. tariffs affect roughly 5% of Canada's exports to the United States, according to trade analysts, but the impact is expected to be concentrated in specific sectors, including wood products and kitchen cabinet manufacturing, industries already under financial strain. Canada's countermeasures, in turn, cover close to 6% of the goods the U.S. exported to Canada last year, based on U.S. trade data, with Canada standing as one of the largest export markets for American goods overall.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, addressing the decision to retaliate, acknowledged the domestic costs involved, saying the move "will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians." Canadian officials have paired the tariff response with a multibillion-dollar support package intended to help affected workers and businesses. Champagne described the government's approach as focused on protecting Canadian industry: "Our dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs as well as a multi-billion dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses."
What Businesses and Consumers Should Watch Before September 8

With just under two weeks before Canada's countermeasures take effect, businesses on both sides of the border are watching for further adjustments to the product list, additional exemptions, or any signal that renewed negotiations between Ottawa and Washington could soften the broader dispute. Companies that rely on cross-border supply chains, particularly in manufacturing, agriculture, and consumer goods, face continued uncertainty over input costs and sourcing decisions as the September 8 deadline approaches.

Economists caution that tariffs of this scale can raise costs for importers and, over time, filter through to consumer prices, though the precise scale of any price effects will depend on how businesses adjust sourcing, absorb costs, or pass them on to customers. For now, the seafood exemption stands as one of the few confirmed adjustments to a retaliatory package that otherwise remains largely intact heading into its scheduled implementation date.

world.title: Jason Arday's Memoir Reaches UK Readers Weeks After His Death and Cambridge Resignation
world.excerpt: Simon & Schuster has published Jason Arday's memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, in the UK, honouring his family's wishes after the sociologist resigned from Cambridge amid plagiarism allegations and was later found dead.
world.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of an open memoir, a university arch and a quiet memorial light

Arday resigned from Cambridge on 5 August 2026 after the university opened a fresh investigation into his qualifications and honorary appointments, following plagiarism allegations tied to his 2015 doctoral thesis.

content.text: Memoir Arrives in UK Bookshops After Weeks of Turmoil

Jason Arday's memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, went on sale in the United Kingdom on Thursday, arriving in bookshops less than two weeks after the sociologist was found dead at a property in Battersea, south London. The book had originally been scheduled for UK release to coincide with a period in which Arday, once celebrated as the youngest Black professor in Cambridge's history, would instead have been fielding questions about a memoir charting his rise from a non-verbal autistic child to a Cambridge professorship. Instead, its publication follows weeks of scrutiny over his academic record, his resignation from the university, and his death.

According to the publisher, Simon & Schuster UK, the book is being released as originally planned, in line with the wishes expressed by Arday's family. The memoir was co-written with Eve Claxton and had already been published in the United States on 11 August, three days before Arday's death.
A Family Statement Breaks Weeks of Silence

In a statement released through Simon & Schuster and reported by the Associated Press and other outlets, Arday's family said he had been unwavering in his desire to see the book published. "To the very end, Jason was clear that he wanted his memoir to be published, and it is only right that we honour his wishes," the family said, adding that much of what had been written about him came from people who did not know "the truth of what he experienced."

The family said they would let the book "speak for itself" and would not comment further on its content, appealing to the media to give them space to grieve. It was, according to reporting from the Times Higher Education and other outlets, the family's first extended public comment since an earlier statement issued immediately after Arday's death, in which they said he had been subjected to a "campaign of sustained abuse" for more than three years.
From a South London Childhood to Cambridge's Youngest Black Professor

Arday's story, as told in the memoir and in earlier profiles including one published by the Guardian in 2023, describes a childhood marked by an autism diagnosis at age three and a period in which doctors doubted he would ever speak, read or live independently. According to publisher materials, Arday did not begin speaking until around age 11 or 12 and did not learn to read and write until his late teens, a turning point he attributes in the book to his now-wife, Debs, who taught him phonics while the two worked together at a South London sporting goods shop.

Arday went on to study physical education at St Mary's University College before moving into academia, holding positions at Durham University and the University of Glasgow before Cambridge announced his appointment as Professor of Sociology of Education in March 2023. At the time, Cambridge described him as a "respected scholar" whose research focused on widening access to higher education for students from minority ethnic backgrounds, and national media reported him as one of the youngest professors in the university's roughly 900-year history.
Plagiarism Allegations Surface and Cambridge Opens an Inquiry

Questions about Arday's academic record began attracting wider attention in mid-July 2026, after British newspapers reported plagiarism allegations concerning his 2015 doctoral thesis, awarded by Liverpool John Moores University. The allegations were first raised by Nathan Cofnas, a US academic and self-described "race realist" who had previously held a research affiliation at Cambridge that ended in 2024 amid accusations of racism. Cofnas alleged that multiple sections of Arday's dissertation had been copied from other works.

content.caption: Editorial illustration · Conceptual artwork; not a documentary photograph.

content.text: Cambridge initially defended Arday, saying the plagiarism allegations had been examined and found to be unfounded. That position shifted on 5 August 2026, when the university announced it had opened a new investigation into Arday's appointment, citing "new information" about his qualifications and honorary appointments. Jesus College, where Arday held a fellowship, said separately that it was launching its own inquiry.
Questions Beyond Academia: Athletic and Fundraising Claims

The scrutiny extended beyond Arday's scholarship to personal claims he had made over the years, including that he ran 30 marathons in 35 days in 2010 to raise money for the homelessness charity Shelter and a children's hospice, a feat that reportedly led to his selection as a torchbearer for the London 2012 Olympics. Some of his stated fundraising and athletic achievements, including a separately reported claim of running 600 miles in six days, came under renewed questioning as journalists examined his public record. British newspapers subsequently noted that some of these claims, including the 600-mile challenge, do not appear in the published memoir.

In an interview with the Times of London published on 1 August, Arday acknowledged making mistakes, which he attributed to his autism and a lack of oversight earlier in his career. He rejected characterisations of himself as "a liar and a fantasist and an academic fraud," saying such accusations were driven by "racism and ableism."
Resignation and the Path to His Death

On 5 August, Arday announced his resignation from Cambridge with immediate effect, in a statement posted on the Good Law Project's website. He described his tenure as "the privilege of my life to teach my students," while saying the years since his appointment had been marked by "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack" that went "far beyond scholarly disagreement."

Nine days later, on 14 August, Arday was found unresponsive at a property in Battersea. The Metropolitan Police said in a statement that his death was being "treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious." Cambridge vice-chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said she was "desperately saddened" by the news. Cambridge has said its investigation into the circumstances of Arday's appointment and tenure will continue, with findings expected to feed into a broader review of how the university appoints senior academics.
A Debate Over Accountability and Proportion

Arday's death prompted an outpouring of tributes alongside a wider debate over responsibility. Some supporters and commentators argued that Cambridge had promoted him too quickly, brushing aside early warning signs in an effort to demonstrate progress on diversity. Others directed criticism at the media, arguing that the volume and tone of coverage was disproportionate to accusations a white academic would likely have faced for comparable errors.
We need to let the investigations proceed, we need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.

That comment came from Cambridge autism researcher Simon Baron-Cohen, who told CNN he had remained in contact with Arday after his resignation and received a final message from him on the morning he died. London Mayor Sadiq Khan described Arday as the victim of a "public shaming," while other public figures, including Diane Abbott and Lord Woolley, used strong language at a vigil in his memory to criticise the press coverage he received. Cofnas, whose research first surfaced the plagiarism claims, was reportedly suspended by Cambridge amid disciplinary proceedings examining his conduct in the case, a move that drew criticism from some academics who argued it threatened academic freedom to scrutinise misconduct.
What the Memoir Does and Does Not Resolve

Great and Unfortunate Things has drawn early attention less for the controversy than for the narrative it offers of neurodivergence, poverty and family devotion, particularly the role of Arday's mother, Giff, in his development. Advance reviews, including from Publishers Weekly, describe it as an account of Arday's path from a non-speaking, illiterate child to a Cambridge professorship, built around the people who supported him along the way. Some observers have noted that the published edition appears to soften or omit certain claims that appeared in earlier drafts or in Arday's public statements over the years, though Simon & Schuster has said it will not comment further on the book's content.

What remains unresolved is Cambridge's formal investigation into how Arday was appointed and what university officials knew, or should have known, about his qualifications before offering him the professorship. The university has not detailed a timeline for concluding that review. The extent to which specific claims in the memoir or in his broader public record are accurate or exaggerated has also not been independently settled, and the family has said it does not intend to engage further with the disputes that surrounded Arday's final months.

world.whyItMatters: The story sits at the intersection of a family’s loss, academic accountability and the press’s duty to verify claims without turning scrutiny into spectacle.
